analysis.title: 'Key Reversal Day' For Bonds... Here's The 'Pain Trade'
key_insights: BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky says 30-year Treasury yields made a new high overnight (by less than 1bp) and then faded about 8bps from intraday highs, which he calls a 'key reversal' day and a sign of exhaustion.

Krinsky still sees the primary trend for rates as higher, but a reversion lower over the next couple of weeks would not be surprising. He says risk/reward for tactical trades is now firmly lower for yields.

Lower yields should help small caps (RTY) stabilize after a drawdown of nearly 10%. Yields finished well off session highs and RTY barely finished off its lows, and in 2007 falling yields coincided with falling RTY in July/August, so the relief is not guaranteed.

A widely read publication ran a cover titled 'Will bonds blow up?' on the morning of the note. Krinsky treats such covers as a contrarian sentiment signal because they tend to appear well after a move is underway.

Krinsky says consensus holds that lower yields are bullish for stocks. He accepts this for small caps (IWM) and equal-weight (RSP), which were hurt by the rise in yields, but questions it for semis and QQQ, which were immune to the surge in rates.
BTIG's 'pain trade' is lower rates together with lower SMH, QQQ and XLK.

RTY/NDX had the 8th lowest RSI on record (12.77) going back to 1985. A fall in yields should support the ratio, but the direction of the move is uncertain. RTY is down about 10% from highs and sits at its 200-day moving average, which more often than not leads to a bounce, so BTIG would not fight it.
BTIG has more conviction that NDX moves lower, and notes few would expect that during a bond rally.

sector_views.rationale: BTIG sees the pain trade as lower SMH, QQQ and XLK if yields fall, since they were immune to the rise in rates and would not benefit from the reversal.

IWM and RSP were punished by the yield surge and could benefit from lower rates. BTIG would not fight a bounce in RTY from its 200-day average, but cites 2007 as a case where falling yields coincided with falling RTY.
